### 2
Your first job is about learning, not proving you already know everything.

- Ask questions early. Share what you’ve tried and where you’re stuck so others can help efficiently.
- Start with small changes. Learn how the team builds, tests, reviews, and deploys code before tackling major improvements.
- Read existing code. Understanding the team’s conventions matters more than using the newest tools.
- Treat code reviews as collaboration, not judgment. Feedback on your code isn’t a verdict on your ability.
- Communicate progress and blockers. A quick update is better than a surprise near a deadline.
- Keep notes and protect your downtime. You’ll learn steadily without needing to work every evening.

Aim to be curious, dependable, and easy to work with. Speed comes with experience.

### 3
Sunlight looks white, but it contains all the colors of the rainbow. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny air molecules that scatter the light in different directions.

Blue light gets scattered much more than red light, so blue light reaches your eyes from all across the sky—not just from the direction of the Sun. That’s why the sky looks blue!

At sunset, sunlight travels through more air before reaching you. Much of the blue light gets scattered away, leaving more reds and oranges to see.

### 2
Your first job is about learning how to contribute reliably—not proving you already know everything.

- Ask questions after making a reasonable attempt yourself. Share what you tried and where you got stuck.
- Start with small changes. Read nearby code, follow existing conventions, and learn how the team tests and deploys.
- Make your work easy to review: keep changes focused and explain why they’re needed.
- Communicate blockers early. A quick heads-up is better than a surprise just before a deadline.
- Treat code review as collaboration, not a verdict on your ability.
- Keep notes on setup steps, unfamiliar concepts, and useful commands.
- Build a sustainable pace. You’ll learn more from consistent work and good rest than from trying to impress everyone with long hours.

You’re not expected to know everything. You are expected to be curious, honest, and willing to learn.

### 3
Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mixture of all the colors in a rainbow. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, it hits tiny molecules of gas that scatter some of the light in different directions.

Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light, so those molecules scatter it much more strongly. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all across the sky, making the sky look blue.

You might wonder why the sky isn’t violet, which has an even shorter wavelength. Sunlight contains less violet, and our eyes are less sensitive to it, so blue is the color we notice most.

Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mixture of colors. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, tiny air molecules scatter some of that light in different directions.
